To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the growth of B16-F1 tumor cells on mouse kidney and lung explants in a low-serumsupplemented medium selects for cells that produce more experimental metastases in syngeneic hosts than the original parental cells, and 2) the growth of 45 B16-F1 clones on lung explants in vitro does not correlate with the metastatic potential of the clones in experimental metastasis assays.
the ability of tumor cell populations to grow on an organ explant is a selective process that does not necessarily lead to the isolation of cells with enhanced metastatic potential.
the metastatic process is a multistep event and that metastases arise from cells that have undergone genetic changes that allow them to adapt to a new organ environment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether metastasis can be regarded as a selective process.
the mechanisms that regulate the metastatic process, with the ultimate aim of finding ways to inhibit the spread of tumor cells to distant organs.
the mechanisms of metastatic dissemination of tumor cells from the primary site and the subsequent growth of these tumor cells in a distant organ.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ability to grow in the organ environment selects out cells with enhanced metastatic potential.
the organ microenvironment is not a selective factor in the metastatic process.

the growth of tumor cells in an organ paren chyma selects for a subset of tumor cells with enhanced ability for growth in this organ and that these cells may be more likely to metastasize in this organ than cells from the parental line.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ability of a cell to grow in an extracellular matrix or in an organ parenchema selects for cells that are more invasive and more likely to form metastases.

the ability of tumor to grow in an extracellular matrix is necessary for tumor metastasis, but the growth of the tumor in the organ parenchymal matrix is not sufficient to select for cells with enhanced metastatic potential.

the ability of a tumor cell to grow in a particular organ microenvironment selects for cells with greater potential to metastasise to that organ, but that the process of selecting for growth in the microenvironment does not necessarily result in a population of cells that is highly metastatic.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ability to grow in a microenvironment is a necessary but insufficient condition for metastatic potential.
metastases are a highly complex and dynamic process that involves many factors and that we need to understand better to be able to treat them.
the metastatic potential of cancer cells is not a static property of the cell but is a property that is acquired and maintained by cells as they grow in the metastatic microenvironment.
